doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Mingus, road life and the jazz economy
title: Studying with Charles Mingus
summary: Mingus gave May formal bass training, visited his home for dinner and duets, and once scared him with a rebuke.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: I see that you spent a little bit of time early on with Charles Mingus?

Yeah I did. Yeah. He was nice enough to teach me, give me some formal training. I love him for that. I still try to give all that knowledge away to young people. I sit back and I say, “Listen, you come to my house and I’ll show you exactly what he told me and how to do it” and all like that. Percy Heath was a student of his also. He was nice enough to teach about a handful of us. A handful. Wonderful technique.
He must have had like different ends of his personality.

I got along with him extremely well. He would come to my house, have dinner, he and his wife, and after dinner he and I would go in the bedroom and play duets. He was really wonderful to me. Really, really nice. He scared the life out of me once though. I mean he really shook me up. ‘Cause he was saying like, “Now when you have a thing like where you’re going to play F seventh to a B flat” — whatever chord — “this is how you would do it.” And I didn’t quite understand, so I said, “Well how would you” I mean I wanted him to demonstrate, you know like say if you were playing in the tune, and that’s what I thought he was going to say. But he said, “What do you mean? You think I’m giving you stuff you’re not going to use?” Really threw me for a loop. But that’s the only time I ever had any kind of run in with him, that he really shook me up, he scared me to death. But I
think I’d have to say, because he always showed me that I was kind of a favorite of his. He was very proud of me, he’d tell people, “Yeah, that’s my student.”
